lead: Today the story of Joseph reaches its climax. Judah, who once proposed selling Joseph, steps forward and offers himself in place of Benjamin; and Joseph can no longer hold back. “I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.” In the Gospel Jesus goes on instructing the Twelve: heal, raise, cleanse, “You received without payment; give without payment.” Both readings are about gift. Joseph gives his brothers a life they did not deserve, and the disciples are to give as a gift what they have received as a gift. Psalm 105 sings the same story from God’s side: he sent a man ahead of them, Joseph, who was sold as a slave.

set: On their second journey to Egypt the brothers brought Benjamin, the youngest, as the governor demanded. Joseph then had his silver cup hidden in Benjamin’s sack and had the brothers arrested on the road, saying that the one in whose sack it was found would become his slave (44:1–17). This was the last test: would they again abandon a favoured brother of Rachel, as they once abandoned Joseph?

Background. Judah’s plea is one of the longest speeches in Genesis. The Lectionary gives it in part, leaving out vv. 22, 23a and 30–34. In the part left out Judah says that he will remain as a slave in Benjamin’s place so that the boy may go home to his father. It is the same Judah who once said, “Come, let us sell him” (37:27). Years ago he spoke of selling a brother; now he offers to be sold himself. The brothers have changed, and this is what Joseph needed to know.
str: 44:18–21, 23b–26: Judah begins humbly and recalls how the governor asked about a father and a brother, and how the brothers refused to leave Benjamin behind.
44:27–29: he quotes the words of old Jacob: one son lost, and the loss of the other would send him to the grave in sorrow.
45:1–3: Joseph cannot control himself; he sends the Egyptians out, weeps aloud and reveals himself, asking first: “Is my father still alive?”
45:4–5: he calls the brothers close and tells them not to be distressed, for God sent him ahead to preserve life.
kw: Judah calls himself “your servant” over and over in this speech, and calls Jacob “your servant my father”. The humility of the word shows how far Judah has come from the man who sold his brother.
Joseph could no longer hold himself back in front of all those who stood by (45:1). The verb means to restrain. Long hidden love breaks through.
Joseph interprets the whole story with this word (45:5). What the brothers meant as death for him, God turned into life for many.
vv: Then Judah stepped up to him and said,

Judah steps forward as spokesman and advocate. In Jewish tradition he becomes the one who takes responsibility, and from his tribe David and, as Matthew’s genealogy says, Jesus will come (Matthew 1:2–3).
his father loves him.
The brothers once hated Joseph because their father loved him more (37:4). Now Judah speaks for the favoured child with love, not envy.
Then Joseph could no longer control himself before all those who stood by him,
The man who has been hard and strange for two chapters breaks. His heart was never closed.
I am your brother, Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.
He names the wrong plainly, without hiding it, and in the next breath he forgives. Forgiveness does not pretend that nothing happened.
for God sent me before you to preserve life.
This is a reading of history in faith: not that the crime was good, but that God was able to use it for life. Verse 8 adds that it was God who sent him.
ch: The Church has read the scene of the discovery as a picture of reconciliation, in which the one who was wronged takes the first step. The Catechism teaches that it is not in our power not to feel an offence, but the heart that offers itself to the Holy Spirit turns injury into compassion and purifies memory by turning hurt into intercession (CCC 2843). The Fathers also saw in Judah, who offers himself in place of Benjamin, a figure of Christ, who gave himself in our place; this is a reading in the tradition, not the sense of the text itself.

set: The mission discourse continues. In yesterday’s verses Jesus named the twelve apostles and began the instructions; today he says what they are to do, what they are to take, and how they are to be received. The setting is the Galilee of the early ministry, where the disciples go out to the villages around them.

Background. The disciples are to travel light: no money in the belt, no bag, no second tunic. The point is not hardship but trust. In Jewish custom a hosting household was a duty of hospitality, and the messenger of a teacher was received as the teacher himself. The greeting of peace (shalom) was the usual greeting on entering a house; here it becomes a gift that can rest or return.
str: vv. 7–8: proclaim the kingdom; heal, raise, cleanse, cast out; what was given as a gift is to be given as a gift.
vv. 9–10: no gold, no bag, no second tunic: the labourer deserves his food.
vv. 11–13: look for a worthy house; greet it; let your peace rest on it, or return to you.
vv. 14–15: if a town will not receive you, shake off the dust; its fate is grave.
kw: The same Greek word is used in Romans 3:24 for the grace by which we are justified, a gift that cannot be earned. Everything the apostles have is gift, so they must not trade on it.
The Greek translates shalom: wholeness, well-being and a right relation with God and neighbour. The disciples carry it with them, and it is not lost if it is refused.
Used for the house, in vv. 11–13. It means a house ready to welcome, not one that has earned the right by merit.
vv: Cure the sick, raise the dead, cleanse the lepers, cast out demons.
The disciples continue the works of Jesus in chapters 8 and 9. The kingdom is announced in word and in deed.
You received without payment; give without payment.
The root of the apostolic ministry: the gift of God cannot be sold. The Church has always taken this word as a warning against making money from sacred things.
for laborers deserve their food.
Those who serve the Gospel may rightly be supported by the community. A similar saying is echoed in 1 Timothy 5:18, and Paul gives the same principle in 1 Corinthians 9:14.
let your peace come upon it; but if it is not worthy, let your peace return to you.
The disciples’ peace is not wasted if it is refused; it returns to them. They carry it as a gift they never lose.
shake off the dust from your feet as you leave that house or town.
A sign of leaving without taking anything away, and without any anger of revenge. The disciples are not to curse a town; they leave its fate with God.
ch: The Catechism, on the sin of simony, recalls that spiritual things cannot be bought or sold, and quotes Peter’s answer to Simon the magician (CCC 2121). The Church applies the word “You received without payment” above all to the sacraments, which are given as gifts of Christ and are not sold. The faithful, for their part, are to provide for the needs of the Church and her ministers, following the word “laborers deserve their food”. The Church has also read the apostles’ lack of means as a call to evangelical poverty and simplicity in every ministry. The warning about Sodom and Gomorrah is a warning to take the word of God seriously; it is not a reason for contempt toward any people.

qa: Does “shake off the dust” mean we should leave anyone who rejects the Gospel?

No. The gesture belongs to the first mission of the Twelve, who were to go on quickly to the next village, and it says that they are not responsible for the choice of those who refuse. Jesus himself never stopped loving those who rejected him, and he told the disciples to forgive (Matthew 18:21–22). Dialogue and patient witness remain the way of the Church.
study: Joseph named the wrong and forgave in the same breath. Is there a wrong I have been unable to speak of, or to forgive?
What gift have I received from God that I am meant to hand on as a gift to others this week?
